archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first, takeaway-fueled)
archetype.definition: A genuinely good Green Bay team built on Jordan Love's passing and a ball-hawking pass defense, carrying a run game that barely functions and a record running slightly ahead of its point differential.

report.headline: Love's arm and a takeaway defense carry a team with no run game
report.take:
This is a passing team with no run game behind it. Jordan Love has started every game and thrown for 2,618 yards, and the pass offense ranks sixth in EPA. The ground game ranks 31st in run EPA at 3.06 yards a carry, with 1.72 yards before contact, also 31st. That last number points at the line, not the backs: MarShawn Lloyd, Kaleb Johnson and Josh Jacobs have all taken real carries, and none of them has found room. The offense lives on Love finding Matthew Golden (92 targets), Christian Watson and Tucker Kraft, and it ranks 27th in success rate because so many early downs on the ground go nowhere.

What changed the season is that the passing game took off. Early on, Love piled up yardage without efficiency: 387 yards in the opener at Minnesota came with negative pass EPA, four sacks and two turnovers. Since then the pass EPA has climbed to 16.9 against Chicago, 11.7 against Carolina and 22.6 in the 45-27 win at New England. The defense has been the other engine. It ranks fifth in pass EPA allowed and fifth in explosive pass rate allowed, and its 19 takeaways rank second, including five against Chicago and four at New England. It has done this without Micah Parsons, who has not played a snap.

The numbers hide a few things. The point differential implies 4.7 wins, not six, and wins over expected (1.32) and a 0.75 one-score win rate both lean toward good fortune. The turnover margin, third in the league, is a sharp turn from last season's slightly negative mark, and takeaway rates rarely hold at this pace. The 26 sacks rank third, but the pressure rate ranks only 20th, so the sack totals are running ahead of the rush that produces them. There are quieter leaks too: the defense ranks 26th in red-zone touchdown rate allowed, special teams rank 26th, and penalties rank 26th. Still, a net EPA ranked seventh says this is not a fluke. The team plays well and has also caught some breaks on top of that.

The road ahead is hard. The NFC North is a four-team scrum, with Chicago at 7-2 and Detroit and Minnesota at 6-2, and the schedule still holds Buffalo, the Rams' fourth-ranked defense, a trip to Chicago and Detroit to close. The injury report is the bigger worry. Both starting tackle Travis Glover and guard Sean Rhyan are out, linebacker Zaire Franklin (a 99% snap player) is out, and Lloyd and Jacobs are both sidelined. A pass offense this good keeps them in the playoff picture, but a thinner line and some takeaway regression make another long winning run harder.

strengths.title: An efficient, accelerating passing game
strengths.body: Love's passing ranks sixth in EPA despite almost no help from the run game. It has grown from a negative opener into a string of strongly positive games, peaking at New England. A protection unit eighth in sack rate gives him enough time. This should hold as long as the line can be patched.

strengths.title: Pass defense that limits and steals
strengths.body: The secondary ranks fifth in pass EPA allowed and fifth in explosive pass rate allowed, so offenses rarely get chunk plays through the air. It also takes the ball away, ranking second in takeaways, all without Parsons. Keeping passes in front of it is sustainable. The takeaway volume is the part likely to cool.

concerns.title: A broken run game getting thinner
concerns.body: The run game ranks 31st in run EPA and 31st in yards before contact, which points to a line that isn't moving anyone. Now starting tackle Glover and guard Rhyan are both out, and Lloyd and Jacobs are sidelined, leaving Kaleb Johnson and possibly Chris Brooks back from IR. This is a real structural flaw, and it puts every drive on Love.

concerns.title: Record and turnovers running hot
concerns.body: Six wins against a differential worth 4.7, plus a top-three turnover margin, means some of this record is fortune. Last season's margin was slightly negative. The sack total (third) sitting well above the pressure rate (20th) is another number likely to drift back. This is not a mirage, but expect the margins to tighten.

concerns.title: Hidden leaks: red zone, kicking, flags
concerns.body: The defense ranks 26th in red-zone touchdown rate allowed, special teams rank 26th in EPA, and the team ranks 26th in penalties. None of these sinks a game alone, but each quietly gives back field position or points in close games. Penalties have improved lately, while the red-zone and special-teams issues look more persistent.

trend.note: After blowout losses to Minnesota and Atlanta in September, the passing game came alive and the only loss since was by three at Detroit, capped by the season-best 45-27 win at New England.

nextGame.headline: Rematch with the league's best defense, minus Kyler Murray
nextGame.body:
This is the rematch of a Week 1 rout: Minnesota won 39-22 in its dome, sacking Love four times and forcing two turnovers while holding his 387 yards to negative pass EPA. The Vikings field the league's top defense by EPA, with the top pressure rate, the top sack rate and the stingiest red-zone touchdown rate. Offenses run against them more than against anyone, and Green Bay is in no position to take that path. Their offense is the weak half, 28th in EPA and 28th in sack rate allowed, which suits a Green Bay pass defense and pass rush that feed on mistakes. The Book makes Green Bay a 4.5-point home favorite with a 41.5 total, which reads like a grind.

Availability tilts both ways. Kyler Murray is out with a hamstring strain, so Carson Wentz, who started Weeks 2 and 9, is likely under center, and receiver Jauan Jennings is also out. Green Bay is missing tackle Travis Glover and guard Sean Rhyan against that pass rush, along with linebacker Zaire Franklin and backs MarShawn Lloyd and Josh Jacobs. Chris Brooks may return from IR. Parsons remains out.

waysToWin.title: Pressure Wentz behind a leaky line
waysToWin.body: Minnesota's line ranks 28th in sack rate allowed, and Green Bay ranks third in sacks and second in takeaways. With Murray out and Jennings inactive, a backup quarterback in obvious passing downs is exactly where this defense gets its strip-sacks and interceptions. Short fields would matter a lot against a defense that rarely gives up long drives.

waysToWin.title: Feed Golden where Minnesota bends
waysToWin.body: For all its dominance, Minnesota ranks 27th in EPA allowed per play to opposing WR1s, while it shuts down tight ends. Golden leads the team in targets by a wide margin, so getting the ball to him quickly beats the rush and targets the one soft spot in the coverage.

waysToWin.title: Win a low-scoring game on ball security
waysToWin.body: Minnesota's offense ranks near the bottom in EPA, so Green Bay does not need a shootout. It needs clean possessions. The offense had no turnovers at New England and has kept the ball safe in its best games. A game in the low 20s favors the team with the better quarterback.

waysToLose.title: Patched line can't hold the rush
waysToLose.body: Minnesota has the league's top pressure rate and sack rate, and Green Bay is missing two starting linemen. Week 1 showed the script: lots of yards, four sacks, two turnovers and drives that died. With no run game to slow the rush, a repeat is the most likely way this goes wrong.

waysToLose.title: Field goals versus a red-zone wall
waysToLose.body: Minnesota allows touchdowns on just a quarter of red-zone trips, the best rate in the league, while Green Bay's own red-zone defense ranks 26th. If the Packers settle for kicks and the Vikings finish their few chances, a game Green Bay controls between the 20s can still slip away.

waysToLose.title: Losing the hidden-yardage battle
waysToLose.body: Minnesota ranks first in special-teams EPA and has the fewest penalties. Green Bay ranks 26th in both. In a game with a total this low, a big return or a drive extended by a flag can decide it.

nextGame.watch: How Green Bay's fill-ins at tackle and guard hold up against the league's best pass rush on early downs, since there is no run game to lean on if they can't.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing game and the pass defense are real, and they should keep Green Bay above .500 and in the wild-card mix. What will regress is the margin: takeaways at this rate, sack totals outpacing pressure, and close-game results all tend to come back toward average. The schedule offers soft spots in New Orleans and Miami but also Buffalo, the Rams' strong defense, a trip to Chicago and Detroit in the finale, so the division race will likely come down to December.

The swing is health. If Glover and Rhyan return quickly and Jacobs is back around his late-November estimate, the run game can at least become survivable, and Love's efficiency should hold. A Parsons return would lift a pass rush that currently converts more than it creates. If the line stays patched, the offense leans even harder on Love, and the record drifts toward the differential.

confidence.note: Nine games with a strong efficiency base, but a heavy injury wave and turnover-driven results add uncertainty.
